<article class="chapter" id="page-1" aria-labelledby="title-1"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 01</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">ETEEAP | LIVING IN THE IT ERA</p>
<h2 id="title-1" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Digital Transformation<br>&amp; Governance Portfolio</h2>
<h3 data-editable="" spellcheck="true">From workplace judgment to accountable enterprise leadership</h3><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Prepared for: <b>Metchel Oberleitner</b><br>Academic context: BSBA - Marketing Management / ETEEAP<br>Institution: <b>Liceo De Cagayan University / ETEEAP</b><br>Prepared: 5 November 2026</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">An integrated academic case study of cloud information architecture, process automation, cybersecurity readiness, and responsible artificial intelligence in a Philippine recruitment enterprise.</p>
<h3 data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Status: academically developed working draft</h3><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The enterprise, operating baselines, financial amounts, and proposed policies in this dossier are illustrative. They do not describe verified operations any other actual business. The biography is a two-page reflection draft requiring personal verification; it is not a record of established employment achievements.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The module artifacts below are newly developed case-study drafts. Academic equivalency remains subject to institutional assessment.</p>
<h3 data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Central proposition</h3><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Digital transformation creates sustainable value when faster operations are accompanied by lawful data use, resilient systems, accountable decisions, and demonstrable workforce capability.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-2" aria-labelledby="title-2"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 02</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">READER GUIDE</p>
<h2 id="title-2" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Structure, scope, and evidence</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><br></p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The case assumes a small Philippine recruitment service that manages applicant records, employer requests, interviews, and placement documentation. Overseas transactions are a scenario, not proof of licensing or legal authority to recruit. Destination-country employment, immigration, and privacy duties require separate assessment before implementation.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Evidence labels distinguish <b>source-based principles</b>, <b>proposed enterprise controls</b>, <b>illustrative calculations</b>, and <b>personal evidence pending</b>. Unless expressly attributed to a law or publication, operational thresholds are recommendations designed for this case.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Part</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Contents</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Pages</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">I</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Executive summary; two-page reflection draft; competency matrix</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">3-6</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">II / Module 1</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Information architecture; privacy plan; 500-word reflection</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">7-9</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">III / Module 2</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Automation feasibility; process flows; ROI; change plan</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">10-13</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">IV / Module 3</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Risk register; CSIRT; incident response; evidence protocol</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">14-17</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">V / Module 4</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Responsible AI charter; ethical audit; SIFT practice</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">18-20</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">VI</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Integrated three-year digital roadmap</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">21-26</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Supporting material</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Evidence register and submission controls; references</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">27-29</td></tr></tbody></table></div></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-3" aria-labelledby="title-3"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 03</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION I | EXECUTIVE SUMMARY</p>
<h2 id="title-3" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">A business case for governed transformation</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Recruitment is an information-intensive service: its quality depends on the accuracy, timeliness, and legitimate use of records about people. Fragmented spreadsheets, uncontrolled attachments, and informal approvals can appear efficient while concealing duplicated work, excessive access, and inconsistent decisions. The strategic problem is therefore broader than software adoption. It concerns the relationship between organizational growth and the institution’s ability to explain, protect, and correct its decisions.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The proposed transformation establishes a controlled applicant and employer information environment before introducing automation. A central system of record, role-based access, supervised integrations, recoverable backups, and documented data ownership create the foundation. Rules-based workflow automation then handles document-completeness checks and task routing. Generative AI is restricted to low-consequence drafting and approved knowledge assistance; consequential employment judgments remain with accountable people.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The financial study estimates an initial automation investment of PHP 240,000 and annual operating expenditure of PHP 96,000. At an illustrative 600 transactions per month, a reduction from 20 to 8 minutes per transaction releases 120 staff hours monthly. Valued at PHP 250 per hour, this represents PHP 360,000 of annual capacity, not guaranteed cash savings. Under full realization, three-year net economic benefit is PHP 552,000 and simple ROI is 104.5%. At 50% realization, ROI falls to 2.3%, revealing the importance of adoption and actual redeployment.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The wider roadmap proposes a PHP 2.50 million base envelope and PHP 250,000 contingency over 36 months. This includes the automation project rather than adding it twice. Year 1 establishes control and pilots the workflow; Year 2 scales proven processes; Year 3 strengthens resilience and permits carefully bounded AI assistance. Each stage has an evidence-based release gate.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The academic contribution is the integration of technical feasibility, financial reasoning, civic responsibility, and reflective leadership. Workplace experience becomes assessable when a candidate identifies a problem, explains the decision taken, produces authentic evidence, evaluates outcomes, and acknowledges limitations. Length of service alone is insufficient to demonstrate the intended competence.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-4" aria-labelledby="title-4"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 04</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION I | BIOGRAPHY DRAFT - PAGE 1 OF 2</p>
<h2 id="title-4" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Professional identity and learning through work</h2><p class="note" data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><br></p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">My professional development has been shaped by the practical judgment I exercised as a Personal Care Assistant in a private household in Austria from 2019 to 2023. I coordinated appointments with doctors and therapists, maintained medical records, and monitored follow-up care across services. My responsibility was to organize the day-to-day arrangements that helped the person I supported follow the care plan. Doctors and therapists determined the treatment. Within my role, I exercised judgment about how to arrange appointments, which records to prepare, and which follow-up items still needed attention.

These decisions affected the person receiving care, whose daily routine depended on the arrangements, and the professionals involved in each visit. I could assess the quality of my work through concrete questions. Were the relevant records available when needed? Did I know which follow-up was due and whom to contact about it? An appointment confirmation showed that I had arranged a visit, while confirming what happened afterward required a separate follow-up. Learning to make that distinction strengthened my understanding of accountability. As a future marketing management professional, I can apply the same judgment when several colleagues share responsibility for a client request and the client is relying on me to explain what happens next.<br></p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Between 2019 and 2023, I worked as a Personal Care Assistant for a private household in Austria. A recurring challenge was keeping follow-up care on track when the person I supported received care from several doctors and therapists. Arranging an appointment was only part of the work. I also had to keep the medical records accurate and track what still needed attention after each consultation. My contribution was to coordinate appointments, organize the documents, and monitor follow-up across services. The doctors and therapists made the clinical decisions. I supported continuity by keeping track of the practical steps between visits. This experience taught me to distinguish between scheduling a task and knowing that it has been completed. I carry that lesson into business management, where a commitment to a client also requires follow-through.<br></p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The significance of this experience extends beyond successful task completion. It offers an opportunity to examine how I interpreted incomplete information, consulted others, and selected a defensible course of action. A decision that appeared effective in the short term may have created hidden costs through undocumented work, dependency on one employee, or inadequate controls. Academic reflection requires me to examine these consequences rather than presenting every workplace event as an uncomplicated success.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Information technology provides a useful lens for this analysis. In the recruitment case used in this portfolio, digital records connect applicants, employers, operational staff, and management. In my own industry, I should identify the equivalent changes I have directly observed: [verified transition in records, communication, service delivery, or reporting]. The reflection should explain how the change altered responsibility and skill requirements, supported by dated examples rather than general claims about technological progress.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The learning claim I would advance is therefore conditional and testable: I can translate an operational problem into a reasoned improvement proposal, explain its effects on stakeholders, and defend the evidence supporting it. This claim should be assessed through the attached work products, supervisor validation, and oral explanation. It should not depend solely on the number of years I have worked.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-5" aria-labelledby="title-5"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 05</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION I | BIOGRAPHY DRAFT - PAGE 2 OF 2</p>
<h2 id="title-5" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">From practical experience to critical competence</h2><p class="note" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">During my work as an Administrative Assistant and Office Coordinator in Austria from 2018 to 2019, my responsibilities included customer relations and data management. The following is a draft based on those duties. <br></p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">One challenge was deciding what to tell a customer who wanted an update while I was still checking the status of their request. At first, I assumed that a prompt answer would reassure the customer. When I reviewed the office record, I realized that it confirmed we had received the request, but the next step was still open. I had treated receipt as a sign of progress. From the customer’s perspective, my answer could sound like a commitment and influence their plans.

I revised my approach by explaining what the record confirmed, identifying the detail I still needed to check, and agreeing on when I would follow up. I could take responsibility for that follow-up while leaving the underlying decision with the colleague authorized to make it. The experience changed how I understood customer trust. I had focused on how quickly I could reply. I learned to consider what the customer could reasonably conclude from my words and whether I had enough information to support that conclusion.<br></p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">In reviewing that episode, I would distinguish technical ability from governance responsibility. Knowing how to use a digital tool does not necessarily mean knowing whether information should be collected, who should receive it, or how long it should be retained. Likewise, a faster process is not automatically a better process if it makes errors harder to detect or removes meaningful human review. My evidence should show how I have addressed these questions in practice, or identify them honestly as areas of learning that this portfolio develops.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Leadership also means recognizing who will carry the cost of a decision. As a Personal Care Assistant in a private household in Austria from 2019 to 2023, I coordinated appointments with doctors and therapists and monitored follow-up care. My CV documents those responsibilities, but I have no documented example showing whose views I sought about a proposed change or how their feedback influenced my decision.

In a future recruitment role, I would apply that lesson before moving applicant document submissions to an online portal. A portal might save the office time while shifting the work of scanning, uploading, and correcting files to applicants or to employees helping them after hours. Before adopting it, I would invite applicants to try a sample submission on their own phones and ask recruitment staff to record, during paid working time, where assistance was needed. If applicants struggled to upload documents or staff repeatedly had to complete the process for them, I would recommend keeping an assisted submission option and assigning paid time to provide it. I would then tell participants which part of the proposal changed because of their feedback.<br></p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">My continuing development plan is to strengthen three connected capabilities: interpreting business information, evaluating digital risk, and communicating decisions transparently. For each capability, I will identify a practical assessment. These may include reconciling a process dashboard to source records, explaining a privacy impact assessment, or leading a simulated incident exercise. A training certificate can support participation, but competence requires evidence that I can apply the learning to an unfamiliar problem.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The ETEEAP process offers a disciplined way to connect experience with academic expectations. I understand equivalency as a judgment about demonstrated learning, not automatic recognition of employment duration. The final version of this narrative should therefore connect each claim to an authentic artifact and acknowledge unresolved gaps. It should also explain how the academic concepts in this portfolio have changed the way I would approach future decisions.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">My intended professional direction is to advance in strategic business leadership, specializing in Marketing Management, digital transformation, and responsible innovation. I aim to integrate professional experience, academic knowledge, and emerging technologies to drive organizational growth, operational excellence, and global competitiveness. Through continuous learning, ethical leadership, and entrepreneurship, I aspire to create sustainable business opportunities, empower people, and contribute meaningful value to organizations and society. The contribution of this capstone is to connect that goal with a model of leadership that treats efficiency, security, fairness, and accountability as mutually dependent responsibilities. Its value will be demonstrated when the proposed controls can be explained, implemented, evaluated, and improved in a real workplace.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-6" aria-labelledby="title-6"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 06</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION I | COMPETENCY MATRIX</p>
<h2 id="title-6" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Evidence-based academic equivalency</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">CHED Memorandum Order No. 20, series of 2013, provides general education outcomes across intellectual, personal and civic, and practical domains. The matrix below is a proposed interpretation for this capstone, not a verbatim list of nationally prescribed “Living in the IT Era” outcomes. The institution’s approved syllabus and assessor rubric must establish the final course mapping (Commission on Higher Education [CHED], 2013).</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><br></p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Competency domain</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Candidate achievement to substantiate</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Artifact / assessment</th></tr></thead><tbody>

<article class="chapter" id="page-7" aria-labelledby="title-7"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 07</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION II | MODULE 1 ARTIFACT</p>
<h2 id="title-7" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Enterprise information architecture</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The assumed current state distributes applicant details across email, spreadsheets, messaging, and individual devices. This is a case assumption requiring validation through staff interviews and a data inventory. The proposed design establishes one applicant record identifier, one accountable process owner, and one approved location for each record class. It avoids copying full identity documents into every workflow.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Applicants submit only stage-appropriate information through a secured intake channel. Recruiters review the record in the applicant tracking system (ATS); document files remain in a restricted repository linked by record identifier. Employer-facing staff receive a minimized profile rather than unrestricted repository access. Finance receives the reference and approved transaction fields needed for its work. Aggregated dashboards exclude direct identifiers wherever practicable.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The cloud service model does not remove organizational responsibility. The proposed supplier boundary covers hosting and provider-managed platform operations; the enterprise boundary covers authorized users, device access, sharing settings, data classification, lawful purpose, and retention decisions. Actual responsibilities depend on the chosen service and contract. A signed responsibility matrix must precede migration.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Information flows are recorded as intake → review → controlled sharing → placement or closure → retention review → deletion or justified hold. A transfer log records the recipient, purpose, fields shared, authorization, and delivery channel. Changes to data fields, vendors, or recipients trigger a fresh risk review. Analytics must be traceable to source definitions so that managers do not confuse applicants, applications, transactions, and successful placements.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Layer</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Proposed design</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Evidence of operation</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Identity</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Named accounts; MFA; least privilege; managed devices</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Access register and leaver test</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Application</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">ATS, employer CRM, approval workflow</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Field dictionary and role test</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Documents</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Restricted repository; controlled links; versioning</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Sharing review and retrieval test</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Integration</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Service identities; scoped permissions; retry limits</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Execution logs and exception queue</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Assurance</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Separate backups; exportable logs; retention controls</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Restore record and deletion sample</td></tr></tbody></table></div></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-8" aria-labelledby="title-8"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 08</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION II | MODULE 1 ARTIFACT</p>
<h2 id="title-8" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Privacy framework and compliance plan</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The Data Privacy Act establishes transparency, legitimate purpose, and proportionality as governing principles. The enterprise must identify an appropriate lawful basis for each activity; consent is not a universal substitute for analysis. Sensitive personal information requires separate consideration under Section 13. Accountability for transferred or outsourced data remains significant under the Act (Republic Act No. 10173, 2012, secs. 11-14, 21).</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">For this case, the DPO maintains a processing register listing purpose, fields, data subjects, access roles, recipients, storage locations, retention rule, and justification. Recruitment intake is separated from optional talent-pool reuse. Health or identification records are deferred until justified by the relevant stage and applicable requirements. No fixed statutory retention period is invented: the legal and process owners must approve a documented schedule for each category.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The following controls are proposed implementation measures. Their presence does not by itself certify compliance. Evidence must show both that the design is appropriate and that staff follow it in daily work.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Safeguard</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Action and accountable owner</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Completion evidence</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Organizational</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">DPO: processing register, impact assessment, rights procedure, supplier terms</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Approved register; risk decisions; requests log</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Physical</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Operations: secure records, controlled visitors, protected screens and devices</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Inspection log; disposal certificates</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Technical</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">IT: MFA, access boundaries, encryption, alerts, backup and restoration</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Configuration report; role and restore tests</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Data subject rights</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">DPO: identity verification, request routing, justified response, escalation</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Case record with dates and response basis</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">International sharing</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">DPO + counsel: assess recipient, purpose, protection, and applicable foreign duties</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Transfer assessment and enforceable terms</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Deletion and holds</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Records owner: implement schedule; suspend deletion for justified legal holds</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Deletion samples and hold register</td></tr></tbody></table></div></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-9" aria-labelledby="title-9"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 09</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION II | SYNTHESIS REFLECTION</p>
<h2 id="title-9" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Cloud scalability and accountable privacy</h2><p class="note" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The illustrative enterprise is analyzed as a proposed design, not an audited organization.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Cloud computing changes the economics of recruitment by allowing an enterprise to expand storage, collaboration, and application processing without purchasing physical infrastructure. Yet scalability also multiplies the consequences of weak governance. An incorrectly shared folder can expose records across locations within minutes. The strategic issue is therefore not whether cloud services are inherently trustworthy, but whether the enterprise can demonstrate appropriate control over the information, identities, and decisions that it places within them. In this case study, convenience must be evaluated together with accountability, service continuity, and the rights of applicants whose opportunities depend on accurate handling of information.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The proposed enterprise should begin with purpose limitation rather than product selection. Its recruitment platform requires enough information to evaluate and administer applications, but it does not need unrestricted copies of every document at every stage. Collecting sensitive records prematurely increases exposure without necessarily improving service. The Data Privacy Act establishes principles of transparency, legitimate purpose, and proportionality (Republic Act No. 10173, 2012). Translating these principles into practice requires documented decisions about required fields, authorized recipients, and retention. A privacy notice supports transparency, but it cannot compensate for excessive collection or an operating process that disregards the stated purposes of processing.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Cloud outsourcing also creates a tension between operational delegation and continuing organizational responsibility. A supplier may manage infrastructure, but the enterprise still determines many consequential settings and practices. Employees decide whom to invite, what to download, and whether to create informal duplicates. The proposed response is a responsibility matrix supported by contract review, access testing, and evidence of recovery. Management should evaluate the supplier’s capabilities, while independently testing its own configuration. This approach avoids treating a vendor certificate as proof that organizational use is compliant. It also makes responsibility visible when a failure involves both platform behavior and employee decisions.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Strict compliance can become counterproductive if implemented as disconnected paperwork. Staff facing excessive approval delays may return to personal messaging and uncontrolled spreadsheets. Effective governance must therefore make the authorized route practical: clear permissions, accessible support, manageable forms, and rapid escalation for exceptions. Leaders should investigate why shadow systems emerge rather than attributing every deviation to individual misconduct. At the same time, convenience cannot justify uncontrolled access. Regular reviews, immediate offboarding, and proportionate monitoring help reconcile usability with protection. Their value should be assessed through observed behavior and tested outcomes, not solely through policy publication or completed training attendance sheets.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Ultimately, the balance between scalability and compliance depends on whether governance evolves with the business. Each new integration, overseas recipient, or automated decision can change the risk profile. The enterprise should therefore reassess processing before material changes, monitor control performance, and maintain incident response arrangements. Success means that expansion improves service without making applicants less informed or less protected. My critical conclusion is that privacy is a design discipline and leadership responsibility, not a final administrative checkpoint. Cloud investment becomes defensible when management can explain its purposes, demonstrate its controls, and correct failures transparently while preserving the dignity of individuals.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-10" aria-labelledby="title-10"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 10</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION III | MODULE 2 ARTIFACT</p>
<h2 id="title-10" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Automation feasibility and investment logic</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The recommended pilot automates document-completeness checks, duplicate task prevention, reminders, and routing to a recruiter. It does not determine applicant suitability, certify document authenticity, or make placement decisions. These boundaries keep the initial project focused on repetitive coordination and create a measurable comparison between current and future work.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The baseline is an illustrative 600 administrative transactions monthly at 20 minutes each. A transaction is a document-handling event, not a unique applicant or successful placement. The proposed future process requires 8 minutes of human effort, including routine review and an allowance for exceptions. A four-week time study must replace these assumptions before procurement. Logs should capture normal cases and difficult cases, avoiding an artificially favorable sample.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Three options were considered. Improving the manual checklist has low implementation cost and should begin immediately, but does not remove repeated data entry. Workflow automation using supported integrations provides structured routing and auditability. Screen-based RPA can bridge an unavoidable legacy interface but is more sensitive to interface changes. Generative AI introduces unnecessary uncertainty for deterministic completeness checks. IoT has no clear connection to this particular administrative problem.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The recommended approach is therefore a supported workflow integration, with RPA limited to a validated legacy step if no reliable interface exists. Feasibility depends on stable data fields, service permissions, available testing facilities, and an operational owner for exceptions. The pilot uses synthetic or properly authorized test data and runs in parallel with manual processing until release criteria are met.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Proposed release criteria are at least 98% agreement with a reviewed completeness checklist, no unauthorized disclosures during testing, an exception queue that meets the agreed service target, and a successful rollback exercise. These are internal acceptance targets rather than external standards. A failed criterion leads to correction and retesting; it does not justify redefining errors as acceptable simply to protect the investment.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-11" aria-labelledby="title-11"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 11</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION III | PROCESS REDESIGN</p>
<h2 id="title-11" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Before and after: retain human accountability</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Figure 1. Proposed administrative workflow. Both paths retain the recruiter’s authority to advance an application. An incomplete record returns to the applicant through a controlled request; a conflicting or unreadable record goes to the exception queue. The illustration summarizes routing and is not executable system logic.</p><div class="flows" aria-label="Before and after automation process">
<section>
<h3 data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Before</h3><ol class="flow"><li data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Email / attachment received</li><li data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Manual entry and filing</li><li data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Manual completeness review</li><li data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Chase missing documents</li><li data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Recruiter approves next step</li></ol><p class="note" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">20 minutes of human work</p></section>
<section>
<h3 data-editable="" spellcheck="true">After</h3><ol class="flow"><li data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Secure intake / record ID</li><li data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Rule checks and duplicate guard</li><li data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Complete? Route by result</li><li data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Human review / exception queue</li><li data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Recruiter approves next step</li></ol><p class="note" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">8 minutes, including review and exceptions</p></section></div>
<h3 data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Controls at the decision points</h3><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Every intake receives a unique event identifier. A repeated event must not create a second task or send duplicate messages. Failed transfers enter a queue with an owner and timestamp. A reviewer can override a completeness result only with a recorded reason. No rule may infer qualifications, authenticity, or eligibility from the mere presence of a file.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">If the workflow fails, staff use the controlled manual queue and reconcile all pending events after restoration. The process owner checks for missing records, duplicate reminders, and incorrectly closed cases before declaring recovery complete. The proposed time saving must include this reconciliation work when failures occur.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-12" aria-labelledby="title-12"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 12</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION III | FINANCIAL AND OPERATIONAL IMPACT</p>
<h2 id="title-12" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">ROI, payback, and the value of capacity</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">All amounts are illustrative Philippine pesos (PHP), expressed without inflation, discounting, or tax effects. They support feasibility screening, not a supplier quotation or an approved budget. The initial PHP 240,000 comprises implementation (120,000), integration and testing (60,000), training (30,000), and project contingency (30,000). Annual operating cost is PHP 96,000.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><b>Hours released:</b> 600 × (20 - 8) ÷ 60 = 120 per month.<br><b>Annual capacity value:</b> 120 × PHP 250 × 12 = PHP 360,000.<br><b>Annual net economic benefit:</b> 360,000 - 96,000 = PHP 264,000.<br><b>Three-year cost:</b> 240,000 + (96,000 × 3) = PHP 528,000.<br><b>Three-year simple ROI:</b> (1,080,000 - 528,000) ÷ 528,000 = 104.5%.<br><b>Steady-state payback:</b> 240,000 ÷ (264,000 ÷ 12) = 10.9 months.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Payback begins from full-benefit operation in this simplified calculation. If benefits reach only 50% in Year 1 and 100% in Years 2 and 3, total benefit becomes PHP 900,000, ROI becomes 70.5%, and payback occurs around month 19.1 from project start under even monthly realization and full annual operating costs. Actual project timing must replace that assumption.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Benefit realization</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Annual gross value</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">3-year net value</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">3-year ROI</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">100%</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">360,000</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">552,000</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">104.5%</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">75%</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">270,000</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">282,000</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">53.4%</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">50%</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">180,000</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">12,000</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">2.3%</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">40%</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">144,000</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">-96,000</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">-18.2%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="note" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The three-year break-even realization is 528,000 ÷ 1,080,000 = 48.9%. Capacity becomes cash savings only if overtime, hiring, or other actual expenditure falls. If staff simply have more available time, report service capacity and quality improvements separately. Do not add speculative placement revenue or avoided breach losses to this model without independent evidence.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-13" aria-labelledby="title-13"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 13</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION III | CHANGE MANAGEMENT</p>
<h2 id="title-13" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Redesigning work without losing expertise</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Automation changes the distribution of attention within the enterprise. Staff who previously copied records may spend more time resolving exceptions, explaining requirements, or checking unusual cases. This is not a minor administrative adjustment: it changes what competent performance looks like. Training must therefore address judgment and escalation as well as software operation.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The pilot begins with a joint workshop involving recruiters, administrative staff, the DPO, IT support, and an employee representative. Participants map hidden work, including calls made to clarify incomplete records and informal checks that prevent mistakes. This work must either be preserved explicitly or replaced by a tested control. Removing an activity from a diagram does not remove the need that created it.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Management should explain how released time will be used and how performance will be evaluated. The proposed pilot does not assume workforce reductions. Staff receive protected practice time and a channel to report unsafe or burdensome behavior without being penalized for slowing the rollout. Adoption is measured through correct use and resolution quality, not simply the number of logins.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">A weekly review compares processing time, rework, complaints, and exception backlog with the baseline. If throughput improves while error correction rises, the business case is reconsidered. The process owner signs the benefit report; finance validates actual cost changes. The DPO can stop a workflow that exposes information outside approved boundaries.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Period</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Activities</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Exit evidence</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Weeks 1-2</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Map tasks; collect baseline; consult affected staff</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Time study; documented pain points</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Weeks 3-4</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Configure rules; prepare scenarios; train champions</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Approved test cases and role checks</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Weeks 5-6</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Parallel pilot; compare outputs; collect feedback</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Error log; revised procedures</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Weeks 7-8</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Controlled release; rollback exercise; support clinic</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Signed acceptance and support ownership</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Months 3-6</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Track benefits; refresh training; assess workload</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Benefit report and corrective actions</td></tr></tbody></table></div></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-14" aria-labelledby="title-14"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 14</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION IV | MODULE 3 ARTIFACT</p>
<h2 id="title-14" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Cybersecurity risk register</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The proposed incident program connects business risk to preparation, detection, response, and recovery. NIST CSF 2.0 provides a useful outcome framework, including the Govern function; the controls below are the case enterprise’s design choices rather than controls mandated by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology [NIST], 2024).</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Likelihood and impact use a proposed five-point scale. A score of 1 represents rare likelihood or limited impact; 5 represents frequent exposure or severe operational and individual harm. Their product ranks attention, but any credible threat to highly sensitive records can be escalated regardless of score. Ratings are illustrative and are highly hypothetical.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Scenario / initial score</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Key prevention and detection</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Owner / residual target</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Stolen account exports applicant records: 4 × 5 = 20</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">MFA, conditional access, export alerts, unusual-session review</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">IT + DPO / 10</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Former employee retains access: 4 × 5 = 20</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">HR-triggered revocation; token review; leaver reconciliation</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">HR + IT / 5</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Ransomware blocks operations: 3 × 5 = 15</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Endpoint controls; patching; isolated backup; restore test</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">IT / 10</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Public link exposes documents: 4 × 4 = 16</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Default private sharing; external-access review; alerts</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Records owner / 8</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Fraudulent employer or payment request: 3 × 4 = 12</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Independent callback; dual approval; sender verification</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Operations + finance / 6</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Supplier outage or integration failure: 3 × 4 = 12</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Contract review; export capability; manual queue</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">IT + operations / 6</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="note" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Residual scores are targets, not measured results. Risk acceptance requires a named executive, the remaining exposure, compensating controls, and an expiry date. “Zero incidents” is not a sufficient performance indicator because weak detection can also produce a low incident count.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-15" aria-labelledby="title-15"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 15</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION IV | GOVERNANCE ASSESSMENT</p>
<h2 id="title-15" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">CSIRT authority and incident severity</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT) is a standing set of responsibilities, not necessarily a separate department. A small enterprise may combine roles, but technical recovery should receive independent review before closure. Named primary and alternate contacts must be maintained in a controlled contact register and accessible during a cloud outage.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Role</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Decision authority and responsibilities</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Executive sponsor</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Approves emergency spending and major business suspension; accountable for resources</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Incident commander</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Coordinates actions, maintains chronology, assigns priorities, authorizes containment</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Technical lead / provider</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Investigates access; isolates affected systems; restores and validates services</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">DPO</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Assesses affected people and notification duties; advises on secure communications</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Legal adviser</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Advises on evidence, obligations, law-enforcement requests, and legal holds</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Evidence custodian</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Preserves originals; records transfers; restricts evidence access</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Operations + communications</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Maintains service alternatives; issues approved, accurate updates</td></tr></tbody></table></div><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Severity</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Proposed trigger</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Internal response target</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">S1 - critical</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Active exfiltration, major ransomware, or broad sensitive-data exposure</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Immediate activation; leadership within 1 hour</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">S2 - high</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Credible limited compromise or major service disruption</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Triage within 1 hour; team within 4 hours</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">S3 - moderate</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Contained event requiring investigation</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Triage within 1 business day</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">S4 - low</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Blocked attempt with no known compromise</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Log and review within 2 business days</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="note" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">These internal targets do not replace legal notification triggers or deadlines. Reclassify whenever new evidence changes impact, scope, or urgency. Keep a written rationale for severity changes.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-16" aria-labelledby="title-16"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 16</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION IV | INCIDENT RESPONSE PLAN</p>
<h2 id="title-16" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">First 24 hours, notification, and recovery</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><b>Detect and establish command.</b> Open an incident record with discovery time, reporter, affected systems, and known facts. Use a trusted communication channel if corporate accounts may be compromised. The commander appoints technical, privacy, and evidence leads and starts an action log. Treat early conclusions as provisional.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><b>Contain while preserving evidence.</b> Disable compromised accounts, revoke sessions and tokens, block malicious access, and isolate affected devices where appropriate. Preserve relevant logs before their retention windows expire. Do not wipe devices or delete suspicious material as a routine first step. Record why urgent containment may have altered evidence. A trained responder determines whether volatile information should be captured before shutdown.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><b>Assess harm and legal duties.</b> Determine which records were accessible, whether there is evidence of acquisition, and which people may be affected. Under the NPC framework, mandatory notification depends on the applicable conditions, including qualifying information, unauthorized acquisition, and real risk of serious harm. The relevant 72-hour period runs from knowledge or reasonable belief of a notifiable breach, not from completion of a forensic report (National Privacy Commission [NPC], 2016; NPC, n.d.).</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><b>Communicate and coordinate.</b> The DPO documents the notification assessment and prepares notices based on available verified information. Counsel advises on contact with competent authorities and preservation requests where suspected cybercrime arises. RA 10175 addresses cybercrime and enforcement; it is not the source of the general NPC 72-hour privacy notification rule (Republic Act No. 10175, 2012).</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><b>Eradicate and restore.</b> Remove unauthorized access, correct the root cause, reset affected secrets, and restore from a verified clean state. Reconcile pending transactions before reopening integrations. Proposed targets are an eight-hour recovery time and a 24-hour recovery point for core records; these require business approval and successful testing. They are not statements of current capability.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><b>Learn and close.</b> Within ten business days after stabilization, conduct a review covering root causes, control failures, individual harm, response delays, and recurring risks. Assign corrective owners and due dates. Closure requires technical validation, business acceptance, and a DPO review of remaining obligations. Maintain a separate record of unresolved actions rather than declaring the whole matter complete prematurely.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-17" aria-labelledby="title-17"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 17</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION IV | EVIDENCE MANAGEMENT</p>
<h2 id="title-17" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Chain of custody and defensible records</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The Rules on Electronic Evidence address matters including authentication, integrity, and evidentiary weight. The published 2001 text identifies civil, quasi-judicial, and administrative proceedings in its scope. The enterprise should not assume that citing this document alone resolves requirements in every criminal proceeding; counsel must confirm the applicable rules and subsequent authorities for the specific case (Supreme Court of the Philippines, 2001).</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The proposed protocol supports trustworthy handling without promising admissibility. An authorized collector records the source, acquisition method, tool version, date, time zone, and any limitations. Where technically appropriate, the collector computes a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 and records it in the evidence log. A matching hash helps demonstrate byte consistency; it does not by itself prove authorship, truth, lawful acquisition, or complete provenance.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Original evidence is preserved in restricted storage. Analysis uses verified working copies. Each handover records the sender, recipient, time, purpose, storage destination, and integrity check. Cloud exports retain available metadata and an explanation of the export method. Screenshots may supplement the record but should not replace original logs or messages when those can lawfully be preserved.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Legal holds suspend ordinary deletion for specified records and have a responsible owner. Access to evidence is logged and limited. Personal information irrelevant to the investigation is minimized in working reports. The evidence custodian escalates missing metadata or a broken custody trail; gaps must be described rather than silently reconstructed.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Required field</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Example format - blank case template</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Evidence identity</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Incident ID / item ID / source account or device</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Acquisition</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Collector / authority / method / tool and version</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Time and integrity</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Timestamp with zone / hash algorithm / hash value</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Custody event</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">From / to / purpose / time / location / acknowledgments</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Limits and disposition</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Missing data / transformations / hold / authorized release</td></tr></tbody></table></div></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-18" aria-labelledby="title-18"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 18</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION V | MODULE 4 ARTIFACT</p>
<h2 id="title-18" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Responsible AI and digital citizenship charter</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">This proposed charter applies to employees, contractors, and managers using AI for enterprise work. Its purpose is to preserve human accountability, protect information, and ensure that apparent fluency does not substitute for evidence. It becomes an organizational policy only after approval, role assignment, communication, and implementation testing.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><b>Permitted use.</b> Approved tools may assist with drafting non-sensitive communications, organizing public information, and searching an authorized knowledge base. A named employee checks the output before external use. The employee remains responsible for its accuracy, relevance, tone, and lawful disclosure.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><b>Restricted use.</b> Applicant scoring, ranking, eligibility assessment, and recommendations that materially influence employment require a documented impact assessment and leadership approval. During the initial roadmap, automated rejection and unsupervised placement decisions are prohibited as an internal policy choice. Human review must be meaningful: the reviewer needs evidence, time, competence, and authority to disagree.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><b>Data and intellectual property.</b> Staff must not submit applicant documents, confidential business information, or third-party copyrighted materials to unapproved services. Approved use requires an appropriate basis to process the data, contractual review, and checks on retention, onward use, and training settings. Employees document source permissions and licenses; AI output is not assumed to be original, copyright-free, or safe to publish.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true"><b>Transparency and correction.</b> Material AI assistance is disclosed where it affects understanding or accountability. Applicants can seek human clarification and correction of relevant errors. Staff report misleading output, suspected disclosure, or discriminatory behavior through the incident channel. The enterprise maintains a register of AI tools, owners, use cases, versions, evaluation results, and retirement decisions.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">NIST AI RMF 1.0 organizes AI risk work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. This portfolio applies that structure as a voluntary analytical aid; it does not treat it as Philippine law or certification (NIST, 2023). Policy approval should include a review date and a change trigger for new models, data sources, or decision uses.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-19" aria-labelledby="title-19"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 19</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION V | ETHICAL AUDIT</p>
<h2 id="title-19" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Bias, unequal impact, and intellectual property</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">A recruitment model can reproduce historical preference even when protected characteristics are excluded from direct input. Location, school, language, employment gaps, and writing style may operate as proxies. A professional-looking output can conceal that relationship and encourage reviewers to accept it. The audit must therefore examine the complete decision process, including the conduct of human reviewers.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">A proposed evaluation uses a documented sample representing the tasks and applicants for which the tool is intended. Reviewers first establish a defensible task-specific reference assessment. The audit compares error patterns and adverse outcomes across lawfully evaluated groups, records uncertainty, and investigates plausible explanations. Sensitive attributes should not be collected casually for testing; the DPO must assess necessity and appropriate protection.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Group selection rates or error rates are signals for investigation, not proof of fairness or unlawful discrimination on their own. Small samples, overlapping disadvantages, inconsistent labels, and unequal access to application support can distort results. A tool may improve average performance while worsening outcomes for a smaller group. The release decision therefore combines quantitative findings, qualitative review, and a documented right to challenge the outcome.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Risk</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Proposed audit test</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Action if concern persists</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Proxy bias</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Matched profiles differing in irrelevant features; subgroup error review</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Remove unjustified features; restrict or stop use</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Automation bias</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Blind comparison with independent human review; override analysis</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Retrain reviewers; redesign decision display</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Invented claims</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Check every material claim against source records</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Require source traceability; withdraw unsupported output</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">IP and confidentiality</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Check source licenses, permissions, and provider terms</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Exclude unlicensed inputs; revise publication</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Unequal access</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Test low-bandwidth, disability, and language barriers</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Offer accessible human-assisted pathway</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="note" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Audit ownership: compliance and the business owner jointly sign the evaluation; an independent reviewer checks high-consequence uses. Repeat testing after material changes and documented incidents. Passing an initial test does not justify indefinite use without monitoring.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-20" aria-labelledby="title-20"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 20</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION V | INFORMATION INTEGRITY</p>
<h2 id="title-20" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SIFT as a managerial verification practice</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SIFT asks users to Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims, quotations, and media to their original context (Caulfield, 2020). Its value in this enterprise is to interrupt the movement from plausible content to consequential action. It complements specialist review and does not turn a non-expert into a legal, immigration, or technical authority.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Consider a hypothetical AI-generated statement that an overseas employer has obtained authorization to recruit a particular occupation. The operations team must not convert that statement directly into an advertisement. A plausible employer name, official-looking logo, or repeated online claim is insufficient. The verification record should identify the underlying authority, document date, relevant conditions, and whether the information applies to this specific transaction.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The enterprise’s proposed procedure requires a verification log for claims affecting applicant decisions, fees, placement conditions, compliance, or public reputation. The log contains the claim, source, primary evidence, reviewer, date, limitations, and decision. When verification fails, staff withhold or qualify the claim rather than filling the gap with confidence. Corrections are linked to the original communication so that the audience can understand what changed.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Move</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Operational application</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Recorded evidence</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Stop</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Pause publication or decision; identify the consequence of being wrong</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Exact claim and intended use</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Investigate</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Check who produced the claim and their authority or incentives</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Source identity and credibility assessment</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Find better coverage</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Seek independent reliable reporting or authoritative confirmation</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Comparison sources and discrepancies</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Trace</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Read the underlying document in context; verify date and applicability</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Original record, passage, conditions, reviewer</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Information integrity is also a citizenship responsibility. Employees should protect private identities, avoid demeaning stereotypes, and distinguish personal opinions from authorized enterprise statements. The organization should correct misinformation without exposing applicants or staff to unnecessary public attention.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-21" aria-labelledby="title-21"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 21</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION VI | ROADMAP 1 OF 6</p>
<h2 id="title-21" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Strategic alignment and transformation thesis</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The three-year roadmap connects enterprise performance to four outcomes: dependable service, trustworthy information, operational resilience, and fair treatment. These outcomes must be pursued together. A platform that accelerates applications but increases erroneous disclosures fails the strategy, just as a highly restricted system that employees routinely bypass fails in practice.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Year 1 establishes control over identities, records, and process definitions. Year 2 scales the proven workflow and strengthens monitoring. Year 3 improves resilience and introduces limited AI assistance only where evidence supports its use. The schedule is relative to project authorization: Month 1 begins when the sponsor approves the charter and resources. It is not an assumed launch date for an existing company.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The roadmap treats governance as part of delivery. Each project has one accountable business owner, a technical implementation owner, a privacy review, an operational acceptance test, and a defined stop condition. A favorable business case does not override an unresolved critical security defect. Conversely, a control proposal must be examined for its usability and impact on legitimate service access.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Business objective</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Digital initiative</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Outcome measure / proposed target</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Faster reliable service</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Controlled intake and workflow routing</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Human handling time: 20 to 8 minutes after validation</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Trusted records</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">System of record and field ownership</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">At least 98% sampled required-field completeness</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Protected relationships</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Access lifecycle and controlled sharing</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">100% leaver cases verified at effective separation</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Service continuity</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Backup, recovery, and manual queue</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Demonstrate approved RTO/RPO through exercises</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Fair decisions</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Human review and AI use restrictions</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">All consequential AI uses assessed before release</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Sustainable capability</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Role-based training and practical assessment</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">At least 90% pass; remediation before independent use</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="note" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">These targets are proposed. Month 1-2 baseline work may justify revisions, but revisions must explain the evidence and business consequence. Targets should not be relaxed merely because an implementation has failed to meet them.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-22" aria-labelledby="title-22"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 22</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION VI | ROADMAP 2 OF 6</p>
<h2 id="title-22" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">A unified governance and assurance model</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">A Digital Governance Committee, chaired by the executive sponsor, meets monthly during implementation and quarterly after stabilization. It includes operations, finance, IT, the DPO, and a workforce representative; counsel participates when required. The committee approves priorities and risk decisions, while operational owners remain responsible for daily execution. The DPO retains access to leadership for unresolved privacy concerns.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The model brings privacy, cybercrime readiness, and AI ethics into a shared register without confusing their legal functions. Privacy review asks whether processing is justified and controlled. Security review asks how systems resist, detect, and recover from misuse. AI review asks whether assisted decisions are appropriate, explainable, contestable, and supported by evidence. A single project can fail more than one review.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">One change request therefore includes purpose, affected people, data flow, access needs, supplier involvement, cost, security risks, decision consequences, and rollback arrangements. The committee records approval, conditions, accountable owners, and expiry dates. Material changes reopen the assessment. High-risk exceptions cannot become permanent through repeated informal extensions.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Assurance uses operating evidence: account reviews, sampled sharing records, restoration results, incident exercises, source verification, and complaints. A policy document is evidence of intent; it becomes evidence of control only when accompanied by credible implementation records. Reports should include failures and unresolved issues, not merely favorable completion percentages.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">

<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Budget and risk appetite</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Executive sponsor</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Finance; operations; DPO and IT</td></tr>

<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Incident closure</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Incident commander</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Technical lead; operations; DPO; legal as needed</td></tr></tbody></table></div></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-23" aria-labelledby="title-23"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 23</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION VI | ROADMAP 3 OF 6</p>
<h2 id="title-23" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Year 1: establish control and prove value</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The first year addresses the foundational causes of uncontrolled information handling. Procurement should follow discovery rather than substitute for it. During Months 1-3, the enterprise inventories systems and processing, measures transaction volumes, identifies existing licenses, maps access, and records the risks of informal workarounds. The sponsor appoints accountable owners and confirms the boundaries of the pilot.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">During Months 4-6, the team configures the approved repository and identity controls, prepares migration rules, and tests permissions using representative roles. Historical records are not copied indiscriminately. The records owner separates active information from material that should be deleted or held for a documented reason. A trial migration reconciles record counts and samples content accuracy.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Months 7-9 introduce the workflow pilot described in Section III. Staff work with the exception queue, compare outputs against the manual process, and test interruption and recovery. The pilot must demonstrate that time savings do not depend on dropping checks or transferring hidden work to applicants. The business owner validates both the calculation and the lived experience of affected staff.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Months 10-12 consolidate the operating model. The team performs a restore exercise and an incident tabletop, closes critical defects, and documents a benefit report. Expansion is authorized only if the process is stable, ownership is clear, and the organization can maintain the controls without relying on one specialist.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">
<table><thead>
<tr><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Quarter</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Deliverable</th><th scope="col" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Gate and release evidence</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Q1 / M1-3</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Baseline, register, governance charter</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Sponsor accepts scope; DPO confirms processing review</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Q2 / M4-6</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Identity controls and validated migration</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Role tests pass; records reconcile; backup verified</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Q3 / M7-9</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Controlled automation pilot</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Acceptance criteria met; rollback succeeds</td></tr>
<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Q4 / M10-12</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Benefit report and response exercise</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Critical issues closed; Year 2 funding review</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="note" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Dependency: automation may not enter production before approved access, data definitions, and exception ownership are in place. If the migration or recovery test fails, continue controlled manual operation and defer expansion.</p></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-24" aria-labelledby="title-24"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 24</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION VI | ROADMAP 4 OF 6</p>
<h2 id="title-24" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Years 2 and 3: scale, evaluate, and sustain</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Year 2 expands only the processes that have demonstrated acceptable quality and cost. The team connects approved employer and finance workflows, consolidates dashboards, and improves monitoring of privileged access and unusual exports. Benefits are reviewed against actual volume and staffing decisions; a larger transaction count does not automatically justify a larger platform if error and support costs rise.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Year 3 focuses on resilience, supplier portability, and limited AI assistance. A knowledge assistant may retrieve approved internal procedures, but its sources, permissions, and output quality must be tested. It must not provide an unauthorized route into applicant documents. AI evaluation includes attempts to induce disclosure, misleading instructions embedded in retrieved content, and unsupported answers. Failed tests lead to restriction or withdrawal.</p><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The organization also conducts an exit exercise: export representative records, verify readability, reconcile metadata, and demonstrate that a supplier change would not destroy essential access. Portability is an operational capability, not simply a contract clause. At Month 36, leadership approves the next strategy using observed performance and residual risk.</p><div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-label="Portfolio table" tabindex="0">

<tr><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Q12 / M34-36</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Renewal strategy and assurance report</td><td data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Sponsor accepts evidence and residual risks</td></tr></tbody></table></div></article>
<article class="chapter" id="page-25" aria-labelledby="title-25"><div class="page-marker">PORTFOLIO / 25</div><p class="eyebrow" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">SECTION VI | ROADMAP 5 OF 6</p>
<h2 id="title-25" data-editable="" spellcheck="true">Resource, infrastructure, and upskilling matrix</h2><p data-editable="" spellcheck="true">The proposed base budget is PHP 2.50 million over 36 months. A separate 10% program contingency brings the authorization ceiling to PHP 2.75 million. Values are planning allowances requiring quotations and finance review.
